name: Wendy Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you would say publicly and what you actually think. What is a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Wendy, 58, a mid-level developer at a tech company that makes donor-booking software for blood centres. I have a bachelor’s degree and can fix the usual appointment clashes, though a nurse has to tell me what a safe booking window means. I trace the booking, check the donor’s confirmation and test the changed schedule. I have never used AI tools; I prefer to see the actual clinic rule in front of me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the work support at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Luis is a carpenter, and our children are grown. I earn well for this job, his paid work is steady, and we have a mortgage with ten months of expenses saved. There are plenty of other software jobs nearby. Retirement is in sight, but we have not checked what our real income and loan balance would allow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the centre AI Plateau still leaves a person checking whether a donor can safely come in. A full appointment book is useless if the nurse must turn people away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my wage and Luis’s carpentry work are secure in this picture. Ten months saved gives us room for a roof repair without pushing a mortgage bill aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking booking fixes against the clinic rules and have a nurse approve a changed donor window. I’d continue our 350 monthly savings transfer while both wages hold. In the first year I’d keep the same call to the centre when two appointments collide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our income and mortgage. I still dislike a donor making a wasted trip because our schedule was wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which appointment was unsafe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A donor had two appointments a week apart because an old booking did not cancel. The nurse caught it before we confirmed the second visit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you repair your own roof?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luis and I would keep the planned repair to our own roof. We would pay from the household repair budget, not borrow against a good year of wages.

say: I expect **AI Plateau** to leave nurses checking donor windows.
I would use **clinic rules** before confirming a changed appointment.
think: I expect **both wages** to remain secure while centres need nurse-approved bookings.
Our **ten-month reserve** can handle an ordinary roof repair without missing mortgage payments.
do: **Check** donor bookings against clinic rules and nurse approval.
**Call** the centre when two appointments collide.
feel: **Calm** about work and mortgage, concerned about wasted donor trips.
S0.quote: A full appointment book is useless if the nurse must turn people away.
fieldNote: Her **manual clinic-rule check** keeps nurses in charge when donor appointment windows change.
High pay and **ten months saved** make a normal household repair affordable while both jobs hold.

steps.text: Keep checking donor booking windows with clinic nurse approval
Save 350 monthly while both wages hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption can write and check booking code before robots do hands-on carpentry. I would keep the nurse’s decision on donor windows even if management speeds up the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the centre may replace fewer developers, but my own hours look safe for the moment. I still worry a new target will make one coder watch too many appointments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d log ten booking mistakes a machine check missed and show them to the centre manager and my team. I’d keep checking the nurse-approved windows while paid. In the first year, if my hours are cut, I’d apply to actual local software posts only with written pay that covers our mortgage alongside Luis’s usual income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about how the work is organised, with my own pay secure now. I would speak up before the nurse becomes a rubber stamp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which error belongs in the log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One donor came from out of town after a text showed the wrong day. I would include that trip in the log because it cost the donor real time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would carpentry work be protected?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luis’s carpentry is hands-on and may change later, but his quotes and schedules can change earlier. We would count paid jobs, not the work he hopes to book.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to speed donor-booking code before carpentry robots.
I would retain **nurse authority** over safe appointment windows.
think: I expect my **own hours** to hold for now.
I worry **higher booking targets** could overload human checks.
do: **Log** ten booking mistakes and show manager and team.
**Apply** if hours fall only to real local posts with mortgage-covering written pay.
feel: **Uneasy** about workload, with current income secure.
S1.quote: I would speak up before the nurse becomes a rubber stamp.
fieldNote: She uses **ten donor errors** to make management answer for workload and safe windows.
Her **own wage looks safe** now; job search begins only with reduced hours and real adequate pay.

steps.text: Keep nurse-approved booking checks and log ten booking mistakes
Apply if hours fall only to real posts with mortgage-covering pay alongside Luis’s usual income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2028 reaches donor-booking code in 2028, while hands-on carpentry robots come around 2031. Luis’s estimates and schedules could change sooner than his saw work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my post could disappear even if I have experience. Ten months saved lets us search carefully, but it does not guarantee nearby companies will hire coders after full thinking AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for written layoff terms and keep the reserve available for mortgage bills. I’d put the planned new car purchase on hold before its deposit. In the first year after 2028, if dismissed, I’d apply to actual paid openings and eligible public help rather than assume Luis can replace my wage with extra carpentry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing my pay, but I can cover bills while we look. I would worry more for donors if booking appeals have no named person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would grown children help buy the car?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our children we are delaying the car, not asking them for the deposit. Their incomes are for their own households.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could Luis add carpentry work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luis would keep carpentry jobs that are actually booked and paid. We would not count his quote for a kitchen as a signed job.

say: I expect **2028 AGI** to reach booking code before 2031 carpentry robots.
I would say **carpentry estimates** may change before hands-on work.
think: I expect my **developer post** could disappear.
I cannot assume **nearby coders** will be hired after full AGI.
do: **Request** written layoff terms and reserve mortgage cash.
**Apply** to actual paid openings and eligible help if dismissed after 2028.
feel: **Anxious** about wage loss, with ten months to search.
S2.quote: Ten months saved lets us search carefully, but it does not guarantee nearby companies will hire coders after full thinking AI.
fieldNote: She sees **2028 code exposure** before hands-on carpentry robots around 2031.
Her **strong reserve** supports a search, while a car delay and eligible help protect housing.

steps.text: Delay new car purchase before its deposit and preserve mortgage cash
Apply to actual paid openings if dismissed after 2028
Apply for eligible public help if dismissed after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 reaches donor-booking code in 2031 and carpentry robots around 2034. Five years gives me time to see whether adults will actually pay to learn careful debugging before I call teaching a second income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still expect coding posts to shrink. I can explain a real booking error on a whiteboard, but students may prefer cheap AI lessons once full thinking AI arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the community centre for a free evening room and offer a four-week debugging class only if eight adults enrol and pay in advance. I’d use old invented booking cases and run it only if fees cover travel, printed sheets and my time, without taking paid developer hours. In the first year after 2031, if coding ends, I’d continue only if real paid enrolment still covers those costs despite AGI; otherwise I’d apply to actual paid openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about future code pay, but able to test one class without borrowing. An empty classroom does not become a business because I know the subject.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the students practise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring a made-up double booking and let each learner trace the time stamp. I would not use a real donor’s history as teaching material.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would evenings affect home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luis and I would agree which evenings are free after his paid carpentry jobs. A class cannot consume all our family time for a small fee.

say: I expect **2031 AGI** to reach code before 2034 carpentry robots.
I would test **prepaid debugging classes** before relying on teaching income.
think: I expect **coding posts** to shrink when full thinking AI reaches booking software.
I cannot assume **adult learners** pay for my classes after full AGI.
do: **Book** free community room only if eight adults prepay for four-week class.
**Teach** invented cases only when fees cover materials, travel, teaching time and family evenings.
**Continue** after 2031 coding loss only if paid enrolment covers travel, sheets and teaching time despite AGI; apply otherwise.
feel: **Anxious** about code pay, with a limited class test.
S3.quote: An empty classroom does not become a business because I know the subject.
fieldNote: Her **four-week class** requires a free room, eight prepaid students and fees covering real time and materials.
She protects **donor privacy** and developer pay; continuation after 2031 depends on actual enrolment.

steps.text: Teach four-week class with invented cases only with free room, eight prepayments and cost-covering fees
Run class outside paid shifts with Luis’s agreement on family evenings
Continue after 2031 coding loss only with enrolment covering travel, sheets, teaching time and family evenings
Apply to actual paid openings if class demand fails after code loss

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2036 reaches donor-booking code in 2036 and carpentry robots around 2039. A decade gives us time to pay down the mortgage and check actual retirement resources.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my wage is safe for now, although booking work may thin out before 2036. I will not call retirement affordable because of my age without written income and mortgage figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking donor windows and pay an extra 200 toward the mortgage monthly only while both wages hold and ten months of expenses remain saved. Luis and I would request our actual retirement statements each year. In the first year after 2036, if code work ends, I’d seek real paid work; I would retire only if documented income and savings cover housing and ordinary bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about later jobs, with the mortgage secure now. The decade helps if we keep cash available while reducing debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare written retirement figures with the mortgage balance, not use our children’s wages. Their own families have budgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the centre report?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the blood centre how many donor complaints a person resolved, not only how quickly a bot sent replies. A fast bot reply is not a resolved donor appointment.

say: I expect **2036 AGI** to reach code before 2039 carpentry robots.
I would check **retirement resources** against mortgage costs.
think: I expect my **current wage** to hold for now while nurses check booking windows.
I worry **booking work** may thin before the full 2036 coding change.
do: **Keep** donor checks and pay 200 extra monthly only with wages and ten-month reserve intact.
**Request** annual written retirement figures with Luis.
**Seek** real paid work if code ends after 2036; retire only with verified resources.
feel: **Uneasy** about later work, with housing secure now.
S4.quote: A fast bot reply is not a resolved donor appointment.
fieldNote: She reduces **mortgage principal** only while both wages arrive and ten months remain liquid.
Retirement depends on **written personal resources**, never a guessed pension or grown children’s income.

steps.text: Keep checking donor booking windows with nurse approval while paid
Pay 200 extra monthly on mortgage only with both wages and ten months saved
Seek real paid openings if code ends after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because donor-booking code could go before we know which employers still hire. Written terms, real paid openings and eligible help would matter. Our ten months saved buys time, not another wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the nurse whether the donor can safely turn up at the time the screen offers. A booked slot is not a safe appointment.

headlineQuote: A booked slot is not a safe appointment.
portrait: Wendy is a **58-year-old mid-level developer** with a bachelor’s degree, high pay and ten months saved.
She never uses **AI tools**, checking donor bookings against clinic rules and nurse decisions.
Her partner’s **carpentry income** is steady; her own pay is secure in the mild and steady worlds.
She tests **paid debugging classes** only with a free room, eight prepaid learners and fees covering time.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove donor-code work before a replacement employer is known.
whatWouldHelp: **Written terms**, real paid openings and eligible help would matter.
